Here we present PhyEvo-Mic-RSI, a physics-guided and expert-informed recursive self-improvement framework that turns one-off human corrections into reusable, verifiable capabilities by updating executable operators, parameters and routing rules with versioned inheritance. Given researcher-defined tasks, the system selects analysis paths from image features without expert labels, while testing and inheriting code updates under fixed budgets. Combining physical priors with expert feedback improves atomic point-defect detection over larger models and raises cross-material interface coverage from 5.13% to 72.11% within a 10% area budget. Adapting the framework to micrographs from unseen studies further separates touching nanoparticles by aligning optimization with particle-level measurements. This work moves computational microscopy beyond standalone models and static scripts towards self-evolving platforms that accumulate human scientific expertise

items.title: Morphological false-vacuum decay in dipolar supersolids
items.summary: False-vacuum decay between two morphologically distinct supersolid phases via bubble nucleation is studied in a uniform dipolar gas confined to the plane. Starting from a metastable honeycomb state, the formation of stripe phase domains is simulated numerically by means of a stochastic projected extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation. The speed of bubble growth is analyzed in relation to the multiple speeds of sound of the supersolid, and is found to be set by the slowest of these sounds. The vacuum decay rate is numerically extracted and compared against a minimal effective model for the Coleman bounce solution connecting the two supersolid orders. Our results establish dipolar supersolids as a novel and versatile platform for studying false-vacuum decay. This setting offers a rich structure of metastable states and collective excitations that come into play in the decay. Furthermore, here, in contrast to previous studies, bubble formation occurs directly in the real-space density and can be probed with \textit{in situ} imaging.

items.title: Neural-network-inferred initial guesses for photoelastic force inversion
items.summary: The inversion of contact forces between closely packed photoelastic disks has become a standard tool in the granular research community. The process iteratively fits the image generated by a forward model to the experimental image, and the correct convergence of the iteration depends critically on the initial guess of the force vectors. In this work, we train a convolutional neural network to infer a force vector from the image in the vicinity of individual contacts. This method, called Contact-Region Inference of Forces, or CRIF, provides the initial guess for the iteration. When tested with synthetic disk images, our approach substantially improves the accuracy of fitting results in comparison to that from the $G^2$ method in the widely adopted PeGS pipeline [Rev. Sci. Instrum. 88, 051808 (2017)], particularly for disks with many contacts and large forces involving high fringe orders. In addition, we extend the method to disks with a built-in axisymmetric residual stress, which often arises when photoelastic disks are submerged in fluids. Finally, on an experimental packing, fits started from the CRIF guess satisfy force reciprocity at strong contacts where fits started from $G^2$ do not.

items.title: A JT/KPZ correspondence
items.summary: We point out a correspondence between the Jackiw--Teitelboim (JT) gravity and the stationary measure of the Kardar--Parisi--Zhang (KPZ) equation on an interval. By relating the Schwarzian limit of the double-scaled SYK to the weakly asymmetric limit of the open ASEP, we establish that the path-integral measure defining the Euclidean evolution between two end-of-the-world branes in JT gravity can be interpreted as the stationary measure of the KPZ equation on an interval with Neumann boundary conditions. We also establish the match between correlation functions.

items.title: Curvilinear nanomagnets of non-trivial geometric topology
items.summary: In this Chapter, we focus on the question of how the global geometric characteristics given by the topology of the sample's shape are reflected in the properties of the magnetization field of the given curvilinear nanoarchitecture. We start with a brief introduction to differential geometry and topology, giving their connection to the specific properties of the vector field represented by the magnetization field defined at the specific manifold. Then we discuss modern fabrication and characterization techniques that make analysis of a sample's topology not only an interesting theoretical concept but also a directly accessible and practically relevant topic. The main attention of the Chapter is dedicated to the theoretical and experimental analysis of nanostructrures with the topology different from the extended films beyond the in-depth studied topic of tubes of the constant radius. In particular, toroidal, spherical, and non-orientable manifolds are considered.
